newsitem.title: USA: FBI reports progress in Saudi bombing probe.
newsitem.headline: FBI reports progress in Saudi bombing probe.

text.p: A senior FBI official said on Wednesday there had been progress in the investigation into the massive truck bombing in Saudi Arabia that killed 19 U.S. servicemen last year.

"I think that eventually we are going to get to the bottom of this. I think we are close already," John Lewis, assistant FBI director for national security, told reporters. "From our standpoint we are beyond the vague point. We are a little bit closer than that," he said of the investigation into the June 25 bombing at the U.S. military housing complex in Dhahran.
Lewis and FBI Deputy Director Bill Esposito declined to comment on Saudi allegations that Iran was responsible for the Khobar Towers attack. Iran has denied any involvement.

"Because of the sensitivity of this whole matter and because of all kinds of international implications we cannot say anything unless we have absolutely confirmed everything. And we are still in that stage," Lewis said. "There's all kinds of speculation, a lot of which is totally incorrect."

FBI chief Louis Freeh and Attorney General Janet Reno in January publicly complained that Saudi Arabia has failed to turn over key information in the investigation. The complaints emerged after FBI agents were not allowed to question Saudi citizens, were not told about arrests there and were unable to get access to all the Saudi evidence.

Asked if there has been a dramatic change since, Lewis said Saudi authorities have been "cooperative" but declined comment on whether FBI agents finally have been given direct access to any of the suspects. "Right now, we're not totally happy, no. But we're making progress," he said.

"The Saudis have cooperated with the FBI on this case more than they have cooperated with any service at any time in their history," he said. "Is that everything we want? Probably not but then again we're the FBI. We want to know everything."

He said the FBI still wanted to talk to Hani Abdel-Rahim Hussein al-Sayegh, who was arrested in Canada last month on the grounds that he represented a security threat. The FBI so far has had no access to Sayegh, who Canada's intelligence service says conducted surveillance at the bombing site and signalled an explosives-laden truck to enter, Lewis said.

Lewis expressed optimism the bombers would be brought to justice in the United States. "I would hope that we are potentially able to get our hands on all of these folks involved in the Khobar bombing."
